explanation: Rain ran through a channel in each figure and out of its mouth, clear of the walls. The name shares a root with 'gargle'; carvings with no spout are strictly grotesques.

claims.text: Gargoyles on medieval churches were carved waterspouts that threw rainwater clear of the walls.
Gargoyles did not hold up roofs, vent chimney smoke or anchor scaffolding.
Rainwater flowed through a channel in a gargoyle and out through its mouth.
The word gargoyle comes from the French gargouille, throat, and shares a root with 'gargle'.
Carved figures on buildings that are not waterspouts are properly called grotesques.
